article_title: Integrated Basic Education and Skills Training (I-BEST)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, September). Integrated Basic Education Skills and Training (I-BEST). https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Six team teaching models for integrating basic skills and occupational instruction
description: I-BEST's signature feature is team teaching, in which a basic skills instructor and an occupational instructor are both present for at least half of instructional time. The report enumerates six forms: "Traditional team teaching", "Collaborative teaching", "Complementary-supportive teaching", "Parallel instruction", "Differentiated split class", and "Monitoring teacher". In the Accelerating Opportunity evaluation all six types were used, with complementary-supportive most popular; in ACE the complementary-supportive model was typical; in the Washington I-BEST study collaborative teaching and two variants of traditional team teaching were implemented.
requirements: Both the basic skills instructor and the occupational training instructor are required to be present in class for at least half of the total instructional time in an I-BEST course
Instructors collaborate to identify joint learning outcomes for students in their class
constraints: The ACE model prescribes a 50 percent minimum of team teaching while Accelerating Opportunity calls for a minimum of 25 percent
target_learners: Adult basic skills students in postsecondary occupational training programs
target_learning_goals: Basic skills in the context of a chosen occupational field
examples: In the Accelerating Opportunity evaluation, all six types of team teaching models were used, with the complementary-supportive model being most popular
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, September). Integrated Basic Education Skills and Training (I-BEST). https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/706

article_title: Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers’ educational beliefs
citation: Voet, M. & De Wever, B. (2018). Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers' educational beliefs. Instructional Science, 46(3), 383-403. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9439-8
title: Three design principles for IBL activities in professional development: authenticity, collaboration, and scaffolded inquiry
description: The IBL activity was designed around three principles. Authenticity meant a discovery-oriented approach using an ill-structured evaluative problem statement requiring students to form their own interpretations of evidence. Collaboration reflected the view that historical reasoning is a social activity in which interaction "stimulates students to elaborate their knowledge". Scaffolding sequenced key inquiry activities in a macro-script within a workflow.
requirements: an ill-structured problem leaving room for different plausible conclusions
sufficient guidance so learners forming their own interpretations from contradictory sources have a positive inquiry experience
constraints: sources were limited to five preselected ones to control the information used
target_learners: student teachers in teacher training programs
target_learning_goals: learning how historical knowledge is constructed
examples: the Peasants' Revolt task posed: "Do you think that 'Peasants' Revolt' is a fitting name for the uprisings that took place in England in 1381?" with five contradictory sources including Wikipedia, a TV documentary, a medieval chronicle and two monographs
key_sources: Voet, M. & De Wever, B. (2018). Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers' educational beliefs. Instructional Science, 46(3), 383-403. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9439-8

article_title: Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony
citation: Qi Li, Die Wang, Weilong Xiao, Yingying Tang, Qi Sun, Binghai Sun & Zhishan Hu. (2024). Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony. npj Science of Learning 9:73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00286-y
title: Interbrain synchrony as the neural foundation of structured teacher-student interaction in flipped classrooms
description: The article proposes that enhanced teacher-student interbrain synchrony (IBS), the temporal coupling of neural systems between individuals in social interaction, underlies the learning benefits of structured interaction. FT alone showed enhanced IBS in left DLPFC, STG, and S1; IBS was higher in the interaction phase of FT; and IBS correlated with learning improvements. The authors state that "IBS serves as its neural foundation" and that the findings "provide neurobiological evidence for the ICAP theory", framing synchrony as reflecting convergence in teacher-student understanding of knowledge.
requirements: fNIRS-based hyperscanning of teacher-student dyads during teaching to measure synchrony
constraints: Preliminary laboratory study with one teacher and one-on-one dyads; the authors encourage future studies to increase the sample size and test real-world classrooms
examples: FT condition dyads showed significantly enhanced class-related IBS in left DLPFC, STG, and S1, while LT and CT conditions did not
key_sources: Qi Li, Die Wang, Weilong Xiao, Yingying Tang, Qi Sun, Binghai Sun & Zhishan Hu. (2024). Structured interaction between teacher and student in the flipped classroom enhances learning and interbrain synchrony. npj Science of Learning 9:73. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00286-y

article_title: The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students’ privacy awareness
citation: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students' privacy awareness. Education Tech Research Dev 72. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10309-x
title: iBuddy simulation system (app, local server, browser client)
description: iBuddy is a 2-hour class simulation in which students install an app to configure a fictional android classmate; the system collects personal data (gallery pictures, contacts, installed apps and usage time) on a local server and generates custom questions displayed to the class to produce a wow effect. The functional architecture is "composed by three parts": a Mobile Client, a local Server, and a Browser Client. The local network is isolated from the internet and all data are deleted during the session.
requirements: An overhead projector is the only required classroom technology beyond the system itself
A presenter and an operator (usually at the local server) run the session
Students without smartphones work in pairs with a classmate
constraints: Data are kept on a local server with no internet connection and deleted about 30 minutes after collection
Without explicit consent the system cannot collect photos or contacts
The operator must exclude embarrassing or illegal content from custom questions
target_learning_goals: awareness that apps access personal data
naming data processes such as customization and advertising
taking specific actions to protect personal data
examples: Between March 2021 and March 2022, 52 sessions were carried out with 978 students in 17 schools; the first 12 sessions tested and fine-tuned the system
key_sources: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students' privacy awareness. Education Tech Research Dev 72. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10309-x

article_title: A Comparison of Internet-Based Learning and Traditional Classroom Lecture to Learn CPR for Continuing Medical Education
citation: Hemmati, N., Omrani, S., & Hemmati, N. (2013). A comparison of internet-based learning and traditional classroom lecture to learn CPR for continuing medical education. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 14(1). https://tojde.anadolu.edu.tr
title: Internet-based CPR CME program with scenario-based simulation, multimedia, and self-assessment delivered via LMS and CD-ROM
description: An interactive Internet-based CME tutorial built on the newest American Heart Association CPR curriculum guidelines and principles of self-directed learning, burned onto CD-ROM and deployed through a university Learning Management System. It incorporated "photography, video, text, narrative and animation" and was organized into three sections: objectives, the CPR algorithm, and "a simple simulation which included examples and Scenario-based with feedback". Pre- and post-tests were automatically uploaded to the LMS, and access was authenticated against an HR database.
requirements: Participants were authenticated through their number and secure password against the HR database, and were required to complete post-assessments to receive CME credit.
constraints: The study examined this particular program in a very specific CME clinical area, which the authors name as a generalization limitation.
target_learners: postgraduate general physician trainees in continuing medical education
target_learning_goals: knowledge of the newest CPR curriculum guidelines and basic life support
examples: The lecture comparison group received the same content "only in terms of text and photography" from a professor given 6 hours, while the IBL group used the multimedia version unscheduled, starting and finishing at any time.
key_sources: Hemmati, N., Omrani, S., & Hemmati, N. (2013). A comparison of internet-based learning and traditional classroom lecture to learn CPR for continuing medical education. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1006264

article_title: Effects of Inquiry-Based Agriscience Instruction on Student Achievement
citation: Thoron, A. C., & Myers, B. E. (2011). Effects of Inquiry–based Agriscience Instruction on Student Achievement. Journal of Agricultural Education, 52(4). https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2011.04175
title: Conceptual model of inquiry-based instruction as interacting student, teacher, and social-cultural components
description: The article's Figure 1 model represents inquiry-based instruction as a set of interactions: significant student-to-student interaction in which learners draw on each other's experiences, student-to-teacher contact in which the teacher acts as facilitator, and teacher preparation, skill, and knowledge. As the article states, "The model represents the interactions taking place in an inquiry–based classroom." The model guided the study's measurement of the inquiry method's effectiveness for knowledge-based achievement.
requirements: Teachers must facilitate learning, have a strong foundation, and know where to guide students to find required information, though they need not know all potentially correct answers
constraints: The model was used to guide one quasi-experimental study in secondary agriscience classrooms
target_learning_goals: communication with peers of different backgrounds
examples: The study measured the effectiveness of all interactions of the model on content knowledge achievement across seven units of instruction
key_sources: Thoron, A. C., & Myers, B. E. (2011). Effects of Inquiry–based Agriscience Instruction on Student Achievement. Journal of Agricultural Education, 52(4). https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2011.04175

article_title: Inquiry Based Teaching in Turkey: A Content Analysis of Research Reports
citation: Aydın Kızılaslan, Mustafa Sözbilir, M. Diyaddin Yaşar. (2012). Inquiry based teaching in Turkey: A content analysis of research reports. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, Vol. 7, No. 4. http://www.ijese.com/
title: Inquiry-based learning grounded in constructivism: students construct knowledge while exploring questions about the natural world
description: The article frames inquiry-based learning (IBL) as a learner-centered approach grounded in constructivism, in which knowledge is constructed in the mind of the learner while individuals possess a question about the natural world and explore answers. IBL is described as "a form of active learning, where assessment deals with how well students develop cognitive skills rather than how much knowledge they possess." The NRC's two uses of inquiry are distinguished: inquiry as content understanding and inquiry as ability. In IBL classrooms, teacher-student and student-student interaction is higher and teachers encourage questioning without judging students' ideas.
requirements: Teachers need to slow down the pace of instruction to motivate student engagement, allow students to understand, analyze, discuss and debate, and avoid telling students what to do or praising, criticizing or rejecting their ideas
target_learning_goals: scientific process skills and inquiry abilities
examples: The article reviews IBL studies in Turkey using this framework to classify research reports by subject, method, sample and data collection tools
key_sources: Aydın Kızılaslan, Mustafa Sözbilir, M. Diyaddin Yaşar. (2012). Inquiry based teaching in Turkey: A content analysis of research reports. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, Vol. 7, No. 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ997153

article_title: Image-based and textbook-based virtual reality training on operational skills among junior residents: a proof of concept study.
citation: Lin Wan-Ni, Chuang Hai-Hua, Chao Yi-Ping, Hsin Li-Jen, Kang Chung-Jan, Fang Tuan-Jen, Li Hsueh-Yu, Lee Li-Ang. (2025). Image-based and textbook-based virtual reality training on operational skills among junior residents: a proof of concept study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07245-0
title: Paired IBVR and TBVR modules for four ORL-HNS procedures built on the ADDIE model
description: Two VR training modules covering image-guided endoscopic sinus surgery navigation, da Vinci transoral robotic surgery, facial nerve detection in parotid surgery, and microscopic tympanostomy. IBVR converts 360° real-patient recordings into an interactive environment via VIVEPAPER, where learners "use hand gestures or controllers to select labeled subsections"; TBVR displays text and photographs on virtual book pages within a 120° field of view. Both were developed following the ADDIE model and reviewed by two experienced instructors.
requirements: A VR head-mounted display with hand controllers; instructional content adapted from authoritative textbooks and manufacturer manuals and verified by two experienced instructors.
constraints: Modules were evaluated only in a controlled artificial environment on a limited set of surgical procedures, which the authors state may restrict generalizability.
target_learners: Junior residents (R1-R2) in otorhinolaryngology-head and neck surgery
target_learning_goals: Precise and proficient preoperative preparation for complex surgeries and performance of basic surgeries
examples: Four 10-minute instructional videos with self-explanation prompts were produced; real-patient demonstrations were recorded with a Garmin VIRB 360 camera.
key_sources: Lin Wan-Ni, Chuang Hai-Hua, Chao Yi-Ping, Hsin Li-Jen, Kang Chung-Jan, Fang Tuan-Jen, Li Hsueh-Yu, Lee Li-Ang. (2025). Image-based and textbook-based virtual reality training on operational skills among junior residents: a proof of concept study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07245-0
